development: The neural tube — the start of the brain and spinal cord — closes, and the placenta begins to form.
heads_up: A home test usually turns positive now. Folic acid matters most in exactly these weeks.

development: The heart tube starts to beat, and the buds that become arms and legs appear.
heads_up: Book a first prenatal visit — most practices see you around week 8.

development: Facial features, eyes and the inner ear begin to take shape.
heads_up: Nausea and fatigue often start here and are usually worst between weeks 6 and 12.

development: Brain cells multiply quickly and the hands and feet emerge as paddles.
heads_up: Sickness can come at any hour — small, frequent snacks tend to help more than big meals.

development: Fingers and toes separate and every major organ is under construction.
heads_up: First prenatal appointment: bloodwork, a dating scan and a confirmed due date.

development: Joints bend, and the heartbeat can often be heard on ultrasound.
heads_up: Ask about prenatal screening options — many are offered from week 10.

development: Officially a fetus now — the vital organs are formed and starting to work.
heads_up: Cell-free DNA screening is available from about now and can also report sex.

development: Fingernails appear and the fetus moves constantly, though you cannot feel it yet.
heads_up: Energy may still be low. It is a demanding trimester even when nothing shows.

development: Reflexes develop and the fetus can open and close its hands.
heads_up: The nuchal translucency scan window is weeks 11–14. Miscarriage risk drops sharply after this point.

development: Vocal cords form and the fetus begins practising breathing motions with amniotic fluid.
heads_up: Second trimester begins — nausea often eases and appetite returns.

development: Facial muscles work: squinting, frowning, grimacing. Fine lanugo hair covers the body.
heads_up: A good stretch for travel if you want any.

development: Bones harden and the fetus can sense light through closed eyelids.
heads_up: You may start to show. Side-sleeping gets more comfortable than lying on your back.

development: The head is upright and the heart pumps around 25 quarts of blood a day.
heads_up: Second-trimester bloodwork is usually offered between 15 and 20 weeks.

development: Fat stores begin forming and the umbilical cord thickens.
heads_up: Round-ligament twinges are common as the uterus grows.

development: Hearing sharpens — voices and heartbeats register. Myelin starts coating the nerves.
heads_up: Talk and read out loud. Familiar voices are recognisable at birth.

development: Vernix, a waxy coating, forms to protect the skin against the amniotic fluid.
heads_up: The anatomy scan is usually 18–22 weeks and sex is often visible there.

development: Halfway. The fetus swallows regularly and starts producing meconium.
heads_up: Measurements switch from crown-to-rump to head-to-heel this week — that is why the length jumps.

development: Movements become the coordinated kicks you can start to feel.
heads_up: First flutters usually land somewhere between weeks 18 and 22.

development: Lips, eyelids and eyebrows are distinct, and the sense of touch develops.
heads_up: Glucose screening is usually scheduled for weeks 24–28.

development: Blood vessels in the lungs develop in preparation for breathing air.
heads_up: Around the viability threshold — outcomes improve week by week from here with neonatal care.

development: Lungs start making surfactant, the substance that keeps the air sacs open.
heads_up: Glucose tolerance window opens. Worth asking what preterm labor feels like.

development: Fat fills out the skin and hair takes on colour and texture.
heads_up: Baby responds to your voice — you may feel a kick when you talk.

development: Eyes open for the first time and the startle reflex appears.
heads_up: Consider a hospital tour and a childbirth class if you want them.

development: Regular sleep and wake cycles begin, with recognisable breathing motions.
heads_up: Last week of the second trimester. Movement patterns start to be worth noticing.

development: The brain surface folds and grooves and blinking begins.
heads_up: Visits usually move to every two weeks. Rh-negative parents get an injection around now.

development: Bones are fully formed but still soft while muscles and lungs keep maturing.
heads_up: Daily movement counts are a simple way to notice change — call about any decrease.

development: Bone marrow takes over red blood cell production and lanugo starts to shed.
heads_up: Heartburn and shortness of breath are common as space runs short.

development: All five senses work and the fetus can turn its head toward light.
heads_up: Braxton Hicks tightenings are normal. Regular painful ones are not — call.

development: Practice breathing is near constant and toenails and real hair are in.
heads_up: Most babies settle head-down around now. A breech position often still turns.

development: The immune system takes on antibodies passed across the placenta.
heads_up: Pack a hospital bag this month — birth from 34 weeks is not unusual.

development: Lungs are nearly ready. A baby born now is late preterm, and usually does well.
heads_up: Group B strep swab is usually done at 36 weeks.

development: Weight gain accelerates to roughly half a pound a week from here.
heads_up: Visits usually become weekly. Confirm the route and any childcare plans.

development: The digestive system is complete and the skull stays soft to ease the passage out.
heads_up: Early term starts at 37 weeks. Learn the signs of labor now.

development: Early term. The brain and lungs keep maturing right through week 39.
heads_up: Every extra week before 39 measurably helps feeding and breathing.

development: Fat continues to build and the grip is firm.
heads_up: Watch for waters breaking, and for contractions getting longer, stronger and closer together.

development: Full term. Brain growth stays rapid right up to birth.
heads_up: Losing the mucus plug can happen days or hours before labor.

development: Ready. Most babies arrive within a week either side of this date.
heads_up: Only about one baby in twenty arrives on the due date. Later is normal.

development: Late term. The placenta keeps working, and is monitored more closely now.
heads_up: Expect extra monitoring and a conversation about induction around weeks 41–42.
